An illustrated Greek manuscript made in Constantinople around 512, a copy of the great 1st-century book on healing plants by the doctor Pedanius Dioscorides, De materia medica. It was a gift to the noblewoman Anicia Juliana, who is shown in a portrait at the front, from people for whom she had built a church.

It has 491 parchment leaves and more than 400 pictures of plants and animals, many painted closely from life. Each plant gets a full page with its name and uses. It is one of the oldest and finest surviving scientific books from the ancient world.

The manuscript stayed in Constantinople for about a thousand years and was still used by doctors there, who added notes in Arabic, Hebrew and Turkish. In the 16th century it was bought for the Holy Roman Emperor and taken to Vienna, where it remains in the Austrian National Library.
